name: Wedding Reception Checklist
description: A planning checklist for the reception covering venue layout, food and drink, timeline, entertainment, decor, toasts, and send-off.

items.text: Confirm the rental window, capacity, and overtime fees.
Choose the floor plan for tables, dance floor, bar, and stage.
Decide on a head table or a sweetheart table for the couple.
Plan guest flow from cocktail hour into the dining space.
Confirm power, parking, restrooms, and accessibility needs.
items.note: Check that the band or DJ has enough outlets and a load-in path.

items.text: Arrange rentals for tables, chairs, linens, and place settings.
Finalize the menu and confirm the dinner service style.
Account for dietary restrictions and allergies.
Plan the bar package and choose a signature cocktail.
Confirm cocktail-hour passed bites and stations.
Order the cake or dessert table and schedule delivery.
Arrange vendor meals for the photographer, band, and staff.
Finalize the guest list and table count.
Build the seating chart once RSVPs are in.
Prepare escort cards or a display seating chart.
Set place cards and any menu cards on tables.
Reserve seats for parents, the wedding party, and special guests.
Create clear signage for the bar, guest book, and gifts.
Draft the reception timeline from entrance to send-off.
Schedule the grand entrance and announcements.
Set times for dinner service and toasts.
Plan the first dance, parent dances, and cake cutting.
Mark when open dancing begins and the bar closes.
Share the run of show with the DJ, caterer, and coordinator.
items.note: Give the emcee or DJ a script with name pronunciations and cues.

items.text: Confirm the band or DJ and their setup needs.
Build a must-play list and a do-not-play list.
Choose songs for the entrance, first dance, and parent dances.
Plan a microphone for toasts and announcements.
Arrange any photo booth, lawn games, or special performances.
Confirm sound and lighting work in the actual space.
Finalize centerpieces and table florals.
Plan lighting such as string lights, uplighting, or candles.
Style the head table, cake table, and entrance.
Add personal touches like photos or a memory table.
Coordinate linens, napkins, and table numbers with your palette.
Confirm who handles setup and teardown of all decor.
Confirm who is giving toasts and the order of speakers.
Remind speakers to keep remarks brief and rehearsed.
Plan the cake cutting and any cultural traditions.
Choose a send-off such as sparklers, bubbles, or petals.
items.note: Check whether your venue permits sparklers or open flames outdoors.

items.text: Arrange transportation for the couple and any guests.
Assign someone to collect gifts, cards, and personal items at the end.

faq.q: How long should a wedding reception last?
faq.a: Most receptions run four to five hours, which comfortably fits the entrance, dinner, toasts, dances, cake, and open dancing with time to spare. Shorter cocktail-style receptions can wrap in three hours. Confirm your venue's rental window early, since overtime fees add up quickly once the party gets going.

faq.q: Buffet or plated dinner for the reception?
faq.a: A plated dinner feels formal and keeps guests seated, but costs more in service staff. A buffet or stations encourage mingling and offer variety, often at a lower price, though lines can form. Family-style sits between the two. Choose based on your budget, formality, and how social you want the meal to feel.

faq.q: What order do reception events go in?
faq.a: A typical flow is the grand entrance, welcome toast, first course or dinner, toasts and speeches, first dance and parent dances, cake cutting, then open dancing and finally the send-off. Adjust the order to fit your venue and energy, but keep speeches near dinner so guests are seated and attentive.

faq.q: How much alcohol do I need for the reception?
faq.a: A common guide is about one drink per guest per hour, with a mix of wine, beer, and spirits. Adjust for your crowd's habits and the time of day. Ask your bartender or venue to estimate quantities, and consider a signature cocktail to simplify the bar and control costs.

faq.q: Do I need assigned seating at the reception?
faq.a: Assigned seating prevents confusion, ensures everyone has a spot, and helps you seat guests with people they will enjoy. For larger or formal weddings it is strongly recommended. Smaller, casual receptions can do open seating. At minimum, reserve a head table or sweetheart table for the couple and key people.
